title: On the Death Anniversary of Former 1st Chief Minister of Andhra pradesh  (Combined CM of Madras Presidency) Tanguturi Prakasam Pantulu
author: sandeepship
content:
Tanguturi Prakasam Pantulu (23 August 1872 – 20 May 1957) was an Indian politician and freedom fighter, chief minister of the Madras Presidency, and subsequently became the first chief minister of the new Andhra state, created by the partition of Madras State along linguistic lines. He was also known as Andhra Kesari (Lion of Andhra). The Andhra Pradesh government issued G.O RT-2500 on 10 August 2014 declaring his birth anniversary a state festival. Andhra Kesari 9 feet Statue in Parliament houses, Statue was Unveiled by Kocheril Raman Narayanan, Presidents of India on 5 May 2000. Andhra Kesari it was the first Biopic Movies on CMs, which was Directed by Vijayachander, It was released on 1 November 1983, the Andhra Pradesh Formation day.

Early life

He was born to Telugu Niyogi Brahmin family of Subbamma and Gopala Krishnayya[1] in the village of Vinodarayunipalem, 26 km from Ongole in Madras presidency (now Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh). When he was 11, his father died and his mother had to run a boarding house at Ongole, a profession that was looked down upon at the time.

When E. Hanumantha Rao Naidu, his teacher at school, moved to Rajamahendravaram, he took Prakasam along with him as that place had better opportunities for education. He acted in Gayopakhyanam by Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham in 1890 along with his teacher.[2] He was interested in becoming a lawyer since childhood, but Prakasam failed his matriculation examination. However, he managed to go to Madras and become a second-grade pleader. Returning to Rajamahendravaram, he eventually became a successful lawyer. He was elected as Municipal Chairman of Rajamahendravaram in 1904 when he was 31 years old. This election was a tough one at that point in time. He was funded for his education by zamindar Kanchumarthi Ramachandra Rao, who was at that time being guarded by raja Vogeti Ramakrishnayya garu, a wealthy landlord and a municipal councelor for a long time and honorary magistrate at Rajamahendravaram whose hierarchy was taken by Ramachandra rao. Prakasam was given utmost support by Ramachandra rao even though they are in opposite sides of politics.

In England

During one of his professional visits to Madras on a court case, a barrister was impressed with his legal acumen and suggested that he become a barrister. As a second-grade pleader, Prakasam could not argue cases at higher courts as only barristers were allowed to do so. Prakasam took the idea to his heart and decided to go to England to pursue legal studies. It was considered a sacrilege to cross the seas during those days. However, as Mahatma Gandhi had done before him, Prakasam made a promise to his mother that he would abstain from eating non-vegetarian food, smoking and drinking. He reached England in 1904. In England, he joined the Royal India Society and worked for the election of Dadabhai Naoroji to the House of Commons.

In the service of public

Prakasam as a Barrister

After completing the barrister course with a certificate of honour in London, Prakasam relocated to Madras high court. He was one of the only Telugu barristers to be successful; until then, most of the successful lawyers were either European or Tamil. He dealt with both civil and criminal cases. Of the latter, one of the important cases was the Ashe murder case. Ashe was the Collector of Tirunelveli and was shot dead in 1907 by Vanchinathan. This was at a time when Bipin Chandra Pal, the nationalist leader from Bengal, was touring the region, making fiery speeches on nationalism. Prakasam defended one of the accused and ensured that he got away with a light sentence. Prakasam also edited Law Times, a legal magazine. The same year he presided over Bipin Chandra Pal's lecture at Madras when others were afraid to come forward, given that the government of the day considered Pal's speeches to border on sedition. He started attending the Congress Party sessions regularly after the Lucknow Pact and signed the Satyagraha pledge in October 1921. He gave up his lucrative law practice. He also started and was the working editor of a newspaper Swarajya (literally self-rule). The paper was published simultaneously in English, Telugu and Tamil.

Prakasam ran a national school and a khādī production centre. He was elected the general secetary of the Congress Party in December 1921 at the Ahmedabad session. Whenever there was unrest or strife such as a riot, he tried to be there so as to comfort people. He visited Punjab during Akali Satyagraha and the Hindu-Muslim riots in Multan. He toured Kerala during the Moplah rebellion despite a ban on visitors from outside the area and had his property at Ooty attached by the government as a consequence. In 1922, during the non-cooperation movement, he organised a demonstration by 30,000 Congress volunteers at Guntur. In 1926, he was elected to the Central Legislative Assembly on a Congress Party ticket.

Andhra kesari appellation and struggle for independence

When the Simon Commission visited India, public decided to boycott it with the slogan "Simon, go back". There were a host of reasons for this boycott, the most important being that the commission did not have a single Indian in its ranks. The commission was greeted with demonstration of black flags wherever it went. When the commission visited Madras on 3 February 1928, Prakasam Pantulu gave the slogan "Go back Simon Commission".The English soldiers warned the demonstrators headed by Prakasam. They threatened to shoot if they (the demonstrators) moved an inch forward. Prakasam Pantulu baring his breast came forward. This made the British soldiers dumb struck. This exemplary courage earned him the title "Andhra Kesari". After this incident, he was known respectfully as "Andhra Kesari" (the Lion of Andhra).

ఇంగ్లండ్ పోయి బారిష్టరయ్యి మద్రాస్ మైలాపూర్ అరవ మేధావులతో పోటీపడి ఆ రోజులలోనే(1917-18 నాటికే)రోజుకు వెయ్యి రూపాయల ఫీజు తీసుకునే స్థాయిలో , కోస్తా జిల్లాలన్నిటిలో భూములు బంగళాలు కొనుగోలు
చేసేటంతగా ఎదిగిన మన కాలపు మేరునగధీరుడు టంగుటూరి ప్రకాశం పంతులు.

గాంధీజీ పిలుపుతో తన ప్లీడరు వృత్తిని వదిలి జాతీయోద్యమంలోకి ఉరికాడు.తన సర్వస్వాన్ని ప్రజాసేవకే అంకితం చేశాడు. లాయర్ గా ఎంతోమందిని
జైళ్ళనుంచి బైటకు తెచ్చిన ఆయన ప్రజలకోసం తాను స్వచ్చందంగా జైలుశిక్షను అనుభవించాడు.గాంధీజీ ఆశయాల ప్రచారం కోసం 'స్వరాజ్య' పత్రికను స్థాపించి గాంధీజీ నిజమైన అనుచరునిగా ఆయన మెప్పును పొందాడు.అదే
గాంధీజీ కొందరి చెప్పుడు మాటలు విని ఆయనను తప్పు పట్టుకుంటే గాంధీజీని సైతం నిలదీశాడు.సైమన్ కమీషన్ కు వ్యతిరేకంగా మద్రాస్ నగరంలో హర్తాళ్ జరిగినప్పుడు తెల్లవాడి తుపాకీకి తన గుండెనే ఎదురు పెట్టాడు.ఆనాటి
ఉమ్మడి మద్రాస్ రాష్ట్రానికి రెవిన్యూ మంత్రిగా,ముఖ్యమంత్రి గా పనిచేశాడు. తెలుగు వారికి ప్రత్యేక రాష్ట్రం ఏర్పడినప్పుడు(1953)తొలి తెలుగు ముఖ్యమంత్రి అయ్యాడు.
దురాశాపరుల మూలంగానూ,శాసన సభ స్పీకర్ తెలివి తక్కువ
తనం మూలంగానూ ఒకే ఒక్క ఓటు తేడాతో ప్రభుత్వం పతనమైనప్పుడు , వ్యతిరేకంగా ఓటువేసిన వారు తమ తప్పు తెలుసుకుని మళ్ళీ ఓటింగ్ కు వెడదామని బ్రతిమాలుకున్నా వినకుండా శాసనసభ నుండి తిన్నగా గవర్నర్
వద్దకు వెళ్ళి తన రాజీనామాను సమర్పించాడు.కేవలం 13 నెలల తన ప్రభుత్వ కాలంలో ఆ రోజుల్లోనే14 నీటి పారుదల ప్రాజెక్టులు స్థాపించాడు.శ్రీ వేంకటేశ్వర విశ్వవిద్యాలయం స్థాపించాడు. తెలుగు వారికి ఓ హైకోర్టు స్థాపించాడు.
తిరుమల తిరుపతి దేవస్థానం నిర్వహణకు కావలసిన మార్పులకు శాసనబద్దత కల్పించాడు.సహకార రంగంలో తెలుగు రాష్ట్రాన్ని ప్రధమ స్థానంలో నిలిపాడు.బెజవాడలో కాటన్ దొర కట్టిన బరాజ్ కొట్టుకుపోయే పరిస్థితి వస్తే ఆనాటి
కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం పైసా కూడ ఇవ్వలేమని స్పష్టం చేస్తే,రాష్ట్ర నిధులనన్నీ మళ్ళించి యుద్ధ ప్రాతిపదికన బరాజ్ ను బాగుచేయించి నిలబెట్టాడు.ఆ భారాన్ని పన్నుల రూపంలో ప్రజలమీద వెయ్యకుండా ఆ లోటును సరిదిద్దాడు.అందుకే
ప్రజలందరూ ఆ బరాజ్ ను ఆయన పేరునే ప్రకాశం బారేజ్ గా పిలుచుకుంటున్నారు.రాష్ట్ర ఏర్పాటు సందర్భంగా దేశంలోనే తొలిసారిగా ఖైదీలందరినీ విడుదల చేశాడు.
అంతటి మహనీయుడు తన చరమ దశలో కటిక
దారిద్ర్యాన్ననుభవించాడు.తనను శాలువతో సత్కరిస్తే 'ఈ శాలువ నాకెందుకురా!ఆ డబ్బుతో అరటిపళ్ళు కొనితెస్తే ఓ పూట గడిచేది కదురా!!' అని తన అనుచరునితో అన్నారంటే ఆయన పరిస్థితి అర్థంచేసుకోవచ్చు.ఆయన మూలంగా
అధికారంలోకి వచ్చిన మహానాయకులందరూ అధికారం కోసం ఆయనకు వెన్నుపోటు పొడిచినా అధికారం కోసం ప్రాకులాడలేదు. 85 సంవత్సరాల వయస్సులో రోహిణీ కార్తె మండుటెండలో వడదెబ్బకు మరణించిన ఇద్దరు
ముదుసలుల కుటుంబ పరామర్శ కోసం వెళ్ళి తాను వడదెబ్బ తిని తెలుగు పౌరుషాన్ని పైలోకాలకు తీసుకుపోయిన "ఆంధ్రకేసరి"టంగుటూరి ప్రకాశం పంతులు గారికి నమస్సులు.

Rajaji with Tanguturi Prakasam

In 1930, when the Congress party wanted all the legislators to resign, he did so but was not convinced about its alternative programme and hence contested and won the by-election. He joined the Congress Party led by Madan Mohan Malaviya but resigned from it as well and persuaded others to do so after Mahatma Gandhi and the Congress Party broke the salt tax law with the Dandi March. Prakasam also resigned as a legislator and was at the forefront in breaking the tax law at Madras. In the meantime, he had to suspend the publication of Swarajya due to the high deposit demanded by the government. It was revived after the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 1931 but it had to be suspended again due to cash flow problems. Unsuccessful attempts were made to restart it again in 1935.

In 1937, Congress Party contested the provincial elections and achieved majority in Madras province, among others. Though Prakasam was in the running for Prime Minister's post, he made way for Rajaji, who returned to active politics as per the wishes of the Congress Working Committee. Prakasam became the revenue minister – his major contribution was the founding and chairing of the Zamindari Enquiry Committee which looked at the structural distortions in agriculture perpetrated due to the Zamindari system followed by the British Government. With the onset of World War II, the Congress ministries resigned from office as they were not consulted by the government about India's participation. Prakasam was the first prominent leader from South India to offer individual satyagraha against the war effort in 1941.

Jawaharlal Nehru with Tanguturi Prakasam

Prakasam was arrested and jailed for more than three years for participating in the Quit India movement of 1942. After his release in 1945, he toured South India to get back in touch with the masses.

Prime Minister of Madras Presidency

In 1946, after the Congress' victory in elections in Madras Presidency, Prakasam became the Prime minister on 30 April 1946, as he and Kamaraj, a Tamil leader, were against Rajaji – the choice of leaders such as Gandhi and Nehru – becoming the Prime minister. However, the government lasted for only 11 months, as it was felt that Prakasam was not accommodating enough to various interests and corruption charges. As Prakasham went against his interest, Mahatma Gandhi faulted Prakasam for accepting gifts and using party funds, ordered Prakasam to resign from congress party.

Prakasam as Premier of Madras Presidency in 1946 with Cabinet Colleagues, Former President of India V V Giri (right side).
Prakasam as Chief Minister of Andhra State in 1953 with Cabinet Colleagues, Former President of India Neelam Sanjiva Reddy (second from right side).

During his tenure as Premier, Prakasam publicly declared his intention to scrap all existing textile industries in the province and replace them with khadi manufacturing and weaving units. In February 1947, Communists broke into a full-scale revolt. On Vallabhbhai Patel's advice, Prakasam responded with widespread arrests and tough crackdown on arsonists.

Post-independence

Prakasam visited Hyderabad State in 1948, while the Nizam was still in power, although Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru warned against doing so because of concern for his personal safety. He met Qasim Rizvi, the leader of the Razakars, and warned him about "pushing his luck too far".

In 1952, he formed the Hyderabad State Praja Party (Hyderabad State People's party) and ensured that all the sitting ministers of the Congress Party were defeated. However, Praja party could not come into power by its own and the coalition that he put together collapsed even before a show of strength could be contemplated.

Meanwhile, in December 1952, Potti Sreeramulu died fasting for the cause of a separate state for the Telugu-speaking people. On 1 October 1953, the state of Andhra was created and Prakasam was unanimous choice for Chief minister of the new state. He was not only the party's choice, but the people's choice too. However, due to corruption charges and opposition from the communists and halting support from the socialists, the government fell after a year. Mid-term elections were held in 1955 by which time Prakasam had more or less retired from active politics. On 1 November 1956, Telugu-speaking parts of the erstwhile Hyderabad State were merged with Andhra State to form Andhra Pradesh. Marathi-speaking parts (Aurangabad region) of the Hyderabad state were merged with Bombay State (which later split into Gujarat and Maharashtra) and Kannada-speaking parts (Gulbarga region) were merged with Mysore State. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy, a future President of India and a staunch follower of Prakasam, became the chief minister. Prakasam was active in touring the state promoting harijan issues (dalit issues). On one such visit to a harijanwada near Ongole, he suffered from severe sunstroke. He was admitted to a Hyderabad hospital and died there on 20 May 1957. His grandson is a bachelor class V employee in Ongole even today and lives with his mother, Annapurnamma (Prakasam's youngest son's wife).

His book The Journey of My Life An Autobiography are available Princeton University Library, One of the top most universities in United states of America.

The Middle kingdoms of India were the political substances in India from the third century BCE to the thirteenth century CE. The period starts after the decrease of the Maurya Empire, and the comparing ascent of the Satavahana line, starting with Simuka, from 230 BCE. The "Center" period went on for around 1500 years and finished in the thirteenth century, with the ascent of the Delhi Sultanate, established in 1206, and the finish of the Later Cholas (Rajendra Chola III, who passed on in 1279 CE).
Outline of South Asian history
Palaeolithic (2,500,000–250,000 BC
Neolithic (10,800–3300 BC)
Chalcolithic (3500–1500 BC)
Bronze Age (3300–1300 BC)
Iron Age (1500–200 BC)
Middle Kingdoms (230 BC-AD 1206)
Late medieval period (1206–1526)
Early modern period (1526–1858)
Colonial states (1510–1961)

This period includes two times: Classical India, from the Maurya Empire up until the finish of the Gupta Empire in the sixth century CE, and early Medieval India from the sixth century onwards. It additionally incorporates the time of traditional Hinduism, which is dated from 200 BCE to 1100 CE. From 1 CE until 1000 CE, India's economy is assessed to have been the biggest on the planet, having between 33% and one-fourth of the world's wealth. It is trailed by the late Medieval period in the thirteenth century.

The Northwest 

Amid the second century BCE, the Maurya Empire turned into a montage of provincial forces with coverage limits. The entire northwest pulled in a progression of intruders between 200 BCE and 300 CE. The Puranas talk about huge numbers of these clans as outsiders and sullied savages (Mlecchas). First the Satavahana line and after that the Gupta Empire, both successor states to the Maurya Empire, endeavor to contain the extensions of the progressive before, in the long run, disintegrating inside due weight applied by these wars.

The attacking clans were affected by Buddhism which kept on prospering under the support of the two intruders and the Satavahanas and Guptas and gives a social extension between the two societies. After some time, the intruders progressed toward becoming "Indianized" as they impacted society and reasoning over the Gangetic fields and were alternately affected by it. This period is set apart by both scholarly and aesthetic accomplishments motivated by social dissemination and syncretism as the new kingdoms straddle the Silk Road.

The Indo-Scythian Sakas

Principle articles: Indo-Scythians and Saka

The Indo-Scythians are a part of the Sakas who relocated from southern Siberia into Bactria, Sogdia, Arachosia, Gandhara, Kashmir, Punjab, and into parts of Western and Central India, Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan, from the center of the second century BCE to the fourth century CE. The main Saka ruler in India was Maues or Moga who built up Saka control in Gandhara and bit by bit broadened matchless quality over north-western India. An indo-scythian guideline in India finished with the remainder of the Western Satraps, Rudrasimha III, in 395 CE.

The intrusion of India by Scythian clans from Central Asia frequently alluded to as the "Indo-Scythian attack", had a huge impact on the historical backdrop of India and also close-by nations. Truth be told, the Indo-Scythian war is only one section in the occasions activated by the itinerant trip of Central Asians from the struggle with Chinese clans which effectively affected Bactria, Kabul, Parthia and India and in addition far away from Rome in the west. The Scythian gatherings that attacked India and set up different kingdoms, included other than the Sakas other partnered clans, for example, the Medes, better source needed Scythians, Massagetae, Getae, Parama Kamboja Kingdom, Avars, Bahlikas, Rishikas, and the Parada Kingdom.

The Indo-Greeks

Primary article: Indo-Greek Kingdom
                                           
Silver coin of the organizer of the Indo-Greek Kingdom, Demetrius (r. c. 205– 171 BC).

The Indo-Greek Kingdom secured different parts of the Northwestern South Asia amid the most recent two centuries BCE, and was managed by in excess of 30 Hellenistic lords, regularly in strife with one another.

The kingdom was established when Demetrius I of Bactria attacked the Hindu Kush right off the bat in the second century BCE. The Greeks in India were in the end isolated from the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom focused in Bactria (now the outskirt among Afghanistan and Uzbekistan).

The articulation "Indo-Greek Kingdom" freely portrays various different dynastic countries. There were various urban communities, for example, Taxila Pakistan's Punjab, or Pushkalavati and Sagala. These urban areas would house various administrations in their occasions, and dependent on Ptolemy's Geography and the terminology of later lords, a specific Theophila in the south was additionally most likely a satrapal or regal seat sooner or later.

Euthydemus I was, as indicated by Polybius a Magnesian Greek. His child, Demetrius, originator of the Indo-Greek kingdom, was hence of Greek plummet from his dad at least. A marriage settlement was organized Demetrius with a girl of Antiochus III the Great, who had halfway Persian descent. The ethnicity of later Indo-Greek rulers is less clear. For instance, Artemidoros Aniketos (80 BCE) may have been of an Indo-Scythian drop. Intermarriage additionally happened, as exemplified by Alexander the Great, who wedded Roxana of Bactria, or Seleucus I Nicator, who wedded Apama of Sogdia.

Amid the two centuries of their standard, the Indo-Greek rulers consolidated the Greek and Indian dialects and images, as observed on their coins, and mixed Greek, Hindu and Buddhist religious practices, as found in the archeological stays of their urban communities and in the signs of their help of Buddhism, indicating a rich combination of Indian and Hellenistic influences. The dissemination of Indo-Greek culture had outcomes which are still felt today, especially through the impact of Greco-Buddhist craftsmanship. The Indo-Greeks eventually vanished as a political element around 10 CE following the intrusions of the Indo-Scythians, despite the fact that pockets of Greek populaces likely stayed for a few centuries longer under the ensuing standard of the Indo-Parthians and Kushan Empire.

The Yavanas

Fundamental article: Yona

The Yavana or Yona individuals, actually "Ionian" and signifying "Western non-native", were depicted as living past Gandhara. Yavanas, Sakas, the Pahlavas and Hunas were now and then depicted as mlecchas, "brutes". Kambojas and the occupants of Madra, the Kekeya Kingdom, the Indus River locale and Gandhara were now and again additionally named mlecchas. This name was utilized to show their social contrasts with the way of life of the Kuru Kingdom and Panchala.

The Indo-Parthians

Fundamental article: Indo-Parthian Kingdom

The Indo-Parthian Kingdom was established by Gondophares around 20 BCE. The kingdom endured just quickly until its triumph by the Kushan Empire in the late first century CE and was a free system where numerous littler dynasts kept up their autonomy.

The Pahlavas 

Fundamental article: The Pahlavas

The Pahlavas are a people made reference to in antiquated Indian writings like the Manusmṛti, different Puranas, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, and the Brhatsamhita. In a few messages, the Pahlavas are synonymous with the Pallava administration of South India. While the Vayu Purana recognizes Pahlava and Pahnava, the Vamana Purana and Matsya Purana allude to both as Pallava. The Brahmanda Purana and Markendeya Purana allude to both as Pahlava or Pallava. The Bhishma Parava of the Mahabharata does not recognize the Pahlavas and Pallavas. The Pahlavas are said to be same as the Parasikas, a Saka gathering. As per P. Carnegy, the Pahlava are most likely those individuals who spoke Paluvi or Pehlvi, the Parthian dialect. Buhler comparatively recommends Pahlava is an Indic type of Parthava signifying "Parthian". In a fourth century BCE, the Vartika of Kātyāyana makes reference to the Sakah-Parthavah, showing a familiarity with these Saka-Parthians, most likely by the method for commerce.

 The Western Satraps

Principle article: Western Satraps

The Western Satraps (35-405 CE) were Saka leaders of the western and focal piece of India (Saurashtra and Malwa: present-day Gujarat, southern Sindh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh states). Their state, or possibly part of it, was designated "Ariaca" as indicated by the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. They were successors to the Indo-Scythians and were contemporaneous with the Kushan Empire, which controlled the northern piece of the Indian subcontinent and was potentially their overlords, and the Satavahana line of Andhra who governed in Central India. They are classified "Western" rather than the "Northern" Indo-Scythian satraps who managed in the territory of Mathura, for example, Rajuvula, and his successors under the Kushans, the "Incomparable Satrap" Kharapallana and the "Satrap" Vanaspara. Although they called themselves "Satraps" on their coins, prompting their cutting-edge assignment of "Western Satraps", Ptolemy's Geography still called them "Indo-Scythians". Altogether, there were 27 autonomous Western Satrap rulers amid a time of around 350 years.

The Kushans 

Fundamental article: Kushan Empire

Kushan Empire

The Kushan Empire (c. 1st– third hundreds of years) initially shaped in Bactria on either side of the center course of the Amu Darya in what is currently northern Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan; amid the first century CE, they extended their domain to incorporate Punjab and a great part of the Ganges bowl, overcoming various kingdoms over the northern piece of the Indian subcontinent in the process. The Kushans vanquished the focal area of the fundamental Silk Road and, in this way, had control of the overland exchange among India, and China toward the east, and the Roman Empire and Persia toward the west.

Ruler Kanishka was an extraordinary supporter of Buddhism; in any case, as Kushans extended southward toward the Indian subcontinent the gods of their later coinage came to mirror its new Hindu majority.

The Indo-Sasanians

Fundamental article: Indo-Sasanians

The ascent of new Persian power, the Sasanian Empire, saw them apply their impact into the Indus locale and overcome lands from the Kushan Empire, setting up the Indo-Sasanians around 240 CE. They were to keep up their impact in the locale until the point when they were ousted by the Rashidun Caliphate. A short time later, they were dislodged in 410 CE by the intrusions of the Hephthalite Empire.

The Hephthalite Hunas 

Fundamental articles: Huna individuals and Hephthalite Empire

Billon drachma of the Huna King Napki Malka (Afghanistan or Gandhara, c. 475– 576).

The Hephthalite Empire was another Central Asian itinerant gathering to attack. They are likewise connected to the Yuezhi who had established the Kushan Empire. From their capital, in Bamyan (present-day Afghanistan) they broadened their standard over the Indus and North India, in this way causing the crumple of the Gupta Empire. They were in the end vanquished by the Sasanian Empire aligned with Turkic people groups.

The Rais

Primary article: Rai tradition

The Rai tradition of Sindh were supporters of Buddhism despite the fact that they additionally settled a gigantic sanctuary of Shiva in Sukkur near their capital, Aror.

The Gandharan Kambojas

Primary articles: Gandhara and Kambojas

The Gandhara Satrapy turned into an autonomous kingdom based from Afghanistan and competed with the Tang tradition, Tibetan Empire, the Islamic Caliphate and Turkic clans for mastery in the district.

The Karkotas

Primary article: Karkota Empire

The degree of the Karkota Empire amid the rule of Lalitaditya Muktapida (eighth century), as per Kalhana's Rajatarangini. Note that Kalhana profoundly overstated the victories of Lalitaditya.

The Karkota Empire was built up around 625 CE. Amid the eighth century, they solidified their standard over Kashmir. The most celebrated leader of the tradition was Lalitaditya Muktapida. As per Kalhana's Rajatarangini, he crushed the Tibetans and Yashovarman of Kanyakubja, and along these lines vanquished eastern kingdoms of Magadha, Kamarupa, Gauda, and Kalinga. Kalhana likewise expresses that he broadened his impact of Malwa and Gujarat and vanquished Arabs at Sindh. According to history specialists, Kalhana profoundly misrepresented the successes of Lalitaditya.

The Kabul Shahis

Principle article: Kabul Shahi

The Kabul Shahi lines ruled parts of the Kabul valley and Gandhara from the decrease of the Kushan Empire in the third century to the mid-ninth century.[30] The kingdom was known as the Kabul Shahan or Ratbelshahan from 565 CE-670 CE when the capitals were situated in Kapisa and Kabul, and later Udabhandapura, otherwise called Hund[31] for its new capital. In antiquated time, the title Shahi gives off an impression of being a very prevalent illustrious title in Afghanistan and the northwestern zones of the Indian subcontinent. Variations were utilized substantially more priorly in the Near East,[32] however too later on by the Sakas, Kushans Hunas, Bactrians, by the leaders of Kapisa/Kabul and Gilgit.[33] In Persian shape, the title shows up as Kshatriya, Kshatriya Kshathiyanam, Shao of the Kushanas and the Ssaha of Mihirakula (Huna chief).[34] The Kushanas are expressed to have received the title Shah-in-shahi ("Shaonano shao") in an impersonation of Achaemenid practice.[35] The Shahis are for the most part up into two times—the Buddhist Shahis and the Hindu Shahis, with the change-over idea to have happened at some point around 870 CE.

The Gangetic Plains and Deccan

Following the death of the Mauryan Empires, the Satavahanas ascended as the successor state to check and fight with the convergence of the Central Asian clans from the Northwest. The Satavahanas straddling the Deccan level likewise gave a connection to the transmission of Buddhism and contact between the Northern Gangetic fields and the Southern areas even as the Upanishads were making progress. In the long run debilitated both by conflict with the northwestern intruders and inner struggle they separated and offered to ascend to a few countries around Deccan and focal India districts even as the Gupta Empire emerged in the Indo-Gangetic Plain and introduced a "Brilliant Age" and resurrection of realm as decentralized neighborhood regulatory model and the spread of Indian culture until fall under the Huna attacks. After the fall of Gupta Empire, the Gangetic district separated into a few states incidentally rejoined under Harsha at that point offering ascend to the Rajput administrations. In the Deccan, the Chalukyas emerged framing an imposing country denoting the relocation of the focuses of social and military power long held in the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the new countries shaping in the southern districts of India.

The Satavahana Empire

Fundamental article: Satavahana line

The Sātavāhana administration started as feudatories to the Maurya Empire however pronounced freedom with its decay. They were the main Indic rulers to issue coins hit with their rulers embellished and are known for their support of Buddhism, bringing about Buddhist landmarks from the Ellora Caves to Amaravathi town, Guntur area. They framed a social scaffold and assumed a fundamental job in exchange and the exchange of thoughts and culture to and from the Gangetic fields toward the southern tip of India.

The Sātavāhanas needed to contend with the Shunga Empire and after that the Kanva dynasties of Magadha to build up their standard. Later they needed to battle in shielding their space from the attacks of Sakas, Yonas, and the Pahlavas. Specifically, their battles with the Western Satraps debilitated them and the realm split into little states.

The Mahameghavahana dynasty

Principle article: Mahameghavahana administration

The Mahameghavahana line (c. 250s BCE-400s CE) was an old decision tradition of Kalinga after the decay of the Mauryan Empire. The third leader of the tradition, Khārabēḷa, vanquished quite a bit of India in a progression of crusades toward the start of the basic era.[36] Kaḷingan military may be reestablished by Khārabēḷa: under Khārabēḷa's generalship, the Kaḷinga state had an imposing sea reach with exchange courses connecting it to the then-Simhala (Sri Lanka), Burma (Myanmar), Siam (Thailand), Vietnam, Kamboja (Cambodia), Borneo, Bali, Samudra (Sumatra) and Jabadwipa (Java). Khārabēḷa drove numerous effective battles against the conditions of Magadha, Anga, the Satavahanas and the South Indian areas administered by the Pandyan tradition (current Andhra Pradesh) and extended Kaḷinga to the extent the Ganges and the Kaveri.

The Kharavelan state had an imposing sea domain with exchanging courses connecting it to Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Borneo, Bali, Sumatra, and Java. Pioneers from Kalinga settled in Sri Lanka, Burma, and also the Maldives and Maritime Southeast Asia. Indeed, even today Indians are alluded to as Keling in Malaysia in view of this.

Albeit religiously tolerant, Khārabēḷa belittled Jainism and was in charge of the spread of Jainism in the Indian subcontinent however his significance is disregarded in numerous records of Indian history. The fundamental wellspring of data about Khārabeḷa is his popular seventeen line shake cut Hātigumphā engraving in the Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves close Bhubaneswar, Odisha. As indicated by the Hathigumpha engraving, he assaulted Rajagriha in Magadha, in this manner prompting the Indo-Greek ruler Demetrius I of Bactria to withdraw to Mathura.

The Bharshiva dynasty 

Principle article: Bharshiva Dynasty

Prior to the ascent of the Guptas, Bharshiva Kings administered the vast majority of the Indo-Gangetic fields. They perform ten Ashvamedha forfeits on the banks of Ganga River. Samudragupta notices Naga rulers in his Allahabad pillar.

The Guptas

Principle article: Gupta Empire

Silver coin of the Gupta King Kumara Gupta I (414– 455).

The Classical Age alludes to the period when a significant part of the Indian Subcontinent was brought together under the Gupta Empire (ca. 320 CE– 550 CE).This period is known as the Golden Age of India and was set apart by broad accomplishments in science, innovation, designing, craftsmanship, argument, writing, rationale, arithmetic, stargazing, religion and reasoning that solidified the components of what is for the most part known as Hindu culture.[44] The decimal numeral framework, including the idea of zero, was developed in India amid this period.[citation needed] The harmony and thriving made under Guptas authority empowered the quest for logical and masterful undertakings in India.

The high purposes of this social inventiveness are seen in Gupta design, form and painting. The Gupta time frame created researchers, for example, Kalidasa, Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Vishnu Sharma, and Vatsyayana who made advances in an assortment of scholastic fields. Science and political organization progressed amid the Gupta era.[citation needed][clarification needed] Trade ties made the locale an essential social focus and set the district up as a base that would impact adjacent kingdoms and areas in Burma, Sri Lanka, and both sea and territory Southeast Asia.

The Guptas performed Vedic penances to legitimize their standard, yet they likewise belittled Buddhism, which kept on giving an option in contrast to Brahmanical orthodoxy.[citation needed] The military endeavors of the initial three rulers - Chandragupta I (ca. 319– 335), Samudragupta (ca. 335– 376), and Chandragupta II (ca. 376– 415) — brought quite a bit of India under their leadership.[48] They effectively opposed the North-Western Kingdoms until the landing of the Hunas who set up themselves in Afghanistan by the primary portion of the fifth century, with their capital at Bamiyan. All things considered, a significant part of the Deccan and southern India were to a great extent unaffected by this condition of motion in the north.

The Vakatakas

Principle article: Vakataka

The stone cut Buddhist viharas and chaityas of Ajanta Caves, worked under the support of the Vakataka rulers.

The Vakataka Empire was the peers of the Gupta Empire and the successor condition of the Satavahanas they framed the southern limits of the north and governed over the present advanced conditions of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra amid the third and fifth hundreds of years. The stone cut Buddhist viharas and chaityas of Ajanta Caves (a UNESCO World Heritage Site), worked under the support of the Vakataka rulers. They were, in the long run, overwhelmed by the Chalukyas.

The Satavahanas (IAST: Sātavāhana), additionally alluded to as the Andhras in the Puranas, were an old Indian tradition situated in the Deccan area. Most present-day researchers trust that the Satavahana administer started in the primary century BCE and kept going until the second century CE, albeit some dole out the start of their manage to as ahead of schedule as the third century BCE. The Satavahana kingdom mostly involved the present-day Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, and Maharashtra. At various occasions, their run reached out to parts of present day Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Karnataka. The tradition had distinctive capital urban areas on various occasions, including Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati (Dharanikota).

The root of the tradition is questionable, however as indicated by the Puranas, their first lord ousted the Kanva administration. In the post-Maurya time, the Satavahanas set up peace in the Deccan area and opposed the surge of remote trespassers. Specifically, their battles with the Saka Western Satraps continued for quite a while. The administration achieved its peak under the govern of Gautamiputra Satakarni and his successor Vasisthiputra Pulamavi. The kingdom divided into little states by the mid-third century CE.

The Satavahanas were early guarantors of Indian state coinage hit with pictures of their rulers. They framed a social extension and assumed a crucial job in exchange and the exchange of thoughts and culture to and from the Indo-Gangetic Plain toward the southern tip of India. They upheld Brahmanism and also Buddhism, and belittled Prakrit writing.

Beginnings 

The date and place of beginning of the Satavahanas, and in addition the significance of the administration's name, involve banter among the antiquarians. A portion of these discussions have occurred with regards to regionalism, with the present-day Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana being differently asserted as the first country of the Satavahanas.

Derivation 

As per one hypothesis, "Satavahana" is a Prakrit type of the Sanskrit Sapta-Vahana ("driven by seven"; in Hindu folklore, the chariot of the sun god is drawn by seven steeds). This would show that the Satavahanas initially guaranteed a relationship with the amazing sun oriented tradition, as was normal in old India. According to Inguva Kartikeya Sarma, the administration's name is gotten from the words sata ("honed", "agile" or "quick") and vahana ("vehicle"); the articulation along these lines signifies "one who rides a deft horse".

Another hypothesis interfaces their name to the prior Satiyaputa tradition. Amazingly, one more hypothesis gets their name from the Munda words Sadam ("pony") and Harpan ("child"), suggesting "child of the entertainer of a steed sacrifice". Several leaders of the tradition bear the name or title "Satakarni". Satavahana, Satakarni, Satakani, and Shalivahana give off an impression of being varieties of a similar word. Damodar Dharmanand Kosambi estimated that "Satakarni" is gotten from the Munda words sada ("horse") and kon ("son").

The Puranas utilize the name "Andhra" or "Andhra-Bhritya" for the Satavahanas. The expression "Andhra" may allude to ethnicity or domain of the line (see Original country underneath). It doesn't show up in the line's very own records.

Unique country

Krishna engraving of lord Kanha in buckle No.19, Nasik caverns. This is the most seasoned known Satavahana engraving, around 100-70 BCE.

The utilization of the name "Andhra" in the Puranas has driven a few researchers to trust that the line began in the eastern Deccan locale (the noteworthy Andhra district, present-day Andhra Pradesh and Telangana). At Kotilingala in Telangana, coins bearing the legend "Rano Siri Chimuka Satavahanasa" were found. Epigraphist and numismatist P. V. P. Sastry at first distinguished Chimuka with the line's organizer Simuka, as a result of which Kotilingala came to be known as the main place where coins ascribed to Simuka were found. Coins credited to Simuka's successors Kanha and Satakarni I were likewise found at Kotilingla. Based on these disclosures, students of history, for example, D. R. Reddy, S. Reddy, and Shankar R. Goyal speculated that Kotlingala was the first home of the Satavahanas. Nonetheless, the coin tests from Kotlingala are little, and it isn't sure if these coins were printed there or come there from someplace else. Moreover, the recognizable proof of Chimuka of Kotilingala with the line's originator Simuka has been challenged by a few researchers including P. L. Gupta and I. K. Sarma, who distinguished Chimuka as a later ruler. P.V.P. Sastry additionally later changed his view and expressed that the two lords were different. As for the Puranas, these writings were gathered significantly later, amid the Gupta time frame, and it isn't sure if the Satavahanas were alluded to as Andhras amid their time.

Naneghat engraving. Dated to 70-60 BCE, in the rule of Satakarni I.

Another area of researchers trusts that the Satavahanas started in western Deccan (present-day Maharashtra). All four surviving engravings from the early Satavahana period (c. first century BCE) have been found in and around this district. The most seasoned known Satavahana engraving was found at Cave No.19 of the Pandavleni Caves in Nashik region and was issued amid the rule of Kanha (100-70 BCE). An engraving found at Naneghat was issued by Nayanika (or Naganika), the dowager of Satakarni I; another engraving found at Naneghat has been dated to a similar period on a paleographic premise. A somewhat later engraving dated to the rule of Satakarni II has been found at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh, situated toward the north of Maharashtra.most of the other Satavahana engravings have additionally been found in western Deccan. Coins credited to Satakarni I have likewise been found at Nashik, Nevasa and Pauni in Maharashtra (other than spots in eastern Deccan and present-day Madhya Pradesh). Based on this proof, a few students of history contend that the Satavahanas at first came to control in the region around their capital Pratishthana (current Paithan, Maharashtra) and afterward extended their region to eastern Deccan. Carla Sinopoli alerts that the surmising about the western Deccan starting point of the Satavahanas is "provisional, best case scenario" given the little example of early inscriptions.

Kanha's Pandavleni makes reference to the term maha-matra (officer-in-control), which demonstrates that the early Satavahanas pursued the Mauryan authoritative model. C. Margabandhu guessed that the Satavahanas were called Andhras on the grounds that they were locals of eastern Deccan (the Andhra district), in spite of the fact that they originally settled their domain in western Deccan in the wake of having filled in as Mauryan subordinates. Himanshu Prabha Ray (1986) restricts this hypothesis, expressing that the Andhra was initially an ethnic term, and did not come to indicate the geological area of eastern Deccan until well after the Satavahana period. According to Vidya Dehejia, the journalists of the Puranas (which were arranged after the Satavahana time frame) mixed up the Satavahana nearness in eastern Deccan as proof for their birthplace in that district, and wrongly marked them as "Andhra".

V. S. Sukthankar guessed that the regional division Satavahani-Satahani (Satavahanihara or Satahani-rattha), in present-day Bellary locale, was the country of the Satavahana family. A stupa in Kanaganahalli town of Karnataka, dated between the principal century BCE and first century CE, highlights limestone boards delineating pictures of Chimuka (Simuka), Satakani (Satakarni) and other Satavahana rulers.

History 

Data about the Satavahanas originates from the Puranas, some Buddhist and Jain writings, the administration's engravings and coins, and outside (Greek and Roman) accounts that attention on trade. The data given by these sources isn't adequate to remake the line's history with supreme assurance. Therefore, there are numerous speculations about the Satavahana chronology.

The Matsya Purana makes reference to that the Andhra line ruled for around 450 years. The Indica of Megasthenes (350 – 290 BCE) makes reference to a ground-breaking clan named "Andarae", whose ruler kept up a multitude of 100,000 infantry, 2,000 mounted force and 1,000 elephants. content:
Pithapuram is a town and a municipality in East Godavari district in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh.

Pithapuram railway station is on the Chennai-Howrah Railway line. Pithapuram is famous for its Ancient Hindu temples. Pithapuram was previously known as Puruhoothika puram (పురుహూతికా పురం) and later known as Pithikapuram (పీఠికా పురం). "Pithapuram is also known as Dakshina Kasi".

The earlist name of Pithapuram was Peetikapuram.The Area passed into the hands of the Vishnukundina during the rule of Vikramendravarma I. They ruled for over two centuries from the first quarter of the 5th Century A.D. The records discovered indicate that their dominion extended over Vishakhapatnam, West Godavari, Krishna and Guntur besides the present East Godavari district. Ranadurjaya, a member of the Durjaya family, ruled pistapuram or Pithapuram as a Vassal of Vikramendravarma in recognition of his services to the State. Another Vishnukundina ruler Indrabhattaraka, defeated the rulers of Vasishta Gotrikas and re-established his authority over this region. His success was, however, short-lived. The early Gangas of Kalinga with the support of some petty rulers, completely routed Indrabhattaraka's army.
This resulted in Vishnukundin's power suffering a severe set-back. Indrabhattaraka was followed on the throne by a few others belonging to the same family. madhavavarma III was the last important ruler of this family. Madhavavarma III was, however, killed in a battle. He was succeeded by his son, Manchannabhattaraka who strove hard to maintain his hold over the ancestral dominion without much success.Every Humanbeing must Watch this place even once in his lifespan

After this Koppula Prolaya Nayaka of the Kapu Caste ruled Pistapuram under the Kakateeya rulers and when the Kakateeyas were defeated. Gaya:-
Gaya Kshetra has acquired lot of prominence in Hindu philosophy and it is dedicated to Pitru Devathas. In many pouranic scripts we find its mention and reference. There are many legends related to Gaya Kshetra and its Mahatmya. Some of them are,

Legend of Gayasura and Vishnu Padam:-

Once upon a time there lived a demon King called Gayasura who was a staunch devotee of Lord Maha Vishnu. Once he did a long penance and when Lord Vishnu appeared before him Gayasura asked him to give a boon so that where he lives would become the most sacred of all the theerthas and also who ever see him or touch him will attain Mukthi (salvation) immediately. The boon was granted by Lord Vishnu accordingly. Because of the boon everybody started attaining Mukthi and this has intruded the jurisdiction of Lord Yama who rules the death.
Then the Trinity Lords approached Gayasura in the guise of Brahmins and asked him for a holy place to perform a sacred Yagna by them. They proposed to perform the Yagna on the body of Gayasura since it was very sacred and celestial by virtue of the boon given by Lord Vishnu which was accepted by Gayasura. The agreement was that the yagna would be held for seven days on the body of Gayasura during which time he was not supposed to get up and deviation of which Gayasura would have to face the death. This was actually a plot to kill him.

Accordingly Gayasura stretched and developed his body and slept on the earth with his head in Gaya of Bihar (Siro Gaya), his Navel portion in Jajpur of Orissa (Nabhi Gaya) and his legs in Pithapuram of Andhra Pradesh (Pada Gaya). The yagna commenced and Gayasura was getting frustrated with the heat of sacred fire but was not moving his body. Six days have past and foreseeing the danger of Gayasura’s success of completing seven days, Lord Shiva took the form of a rooster and crowed at midnight. Assuming it as a wake up call in the morning Gayasura woke up and the Yagna got destroyed. Then the three Brahmins revealed their original form and Lord Vishnu told Gayasura that now he had to be killed and accordingly stepped his foot on the chest of Gayasura and subdued him.

There is also another version “As Gayasura started getting disturbed the Deities kept a big stone called Dharmashila on the head of Gayasura and all of them stood on it. Besides they also requested Lord Maha Vishnu to keep his foot on the stone so that he would not get up. Accordingly Lord Vishnu stepped on him with his foot and Gayasura started slowly succumbing to the pressure.”

Before killing Lord Vishnu granted him Mukthi and gave him a boon that his body would become a sacrosanct place for performing sacred rites for departed souls and the place would get immortalized in his name. On request of Gayasura He also gave a boon that who ever perform ancestral rites at this place and offer Pindas on his body site their ancestors would get salvation besides the people performing the rites and touching the spot. There is also a belief that Lord Maha Vishnu while answering one of Gayasura’s queries had said that the day Pindas stop falling in his mouth that day he can get up. But since then there is a continuous flow of Pindas falling at this spot and there is no stop to the rituals.

It is the same foot print of Lord Maha Vishnu that is being worshipped today and on which sacred Pindas are being offered by the pilgrims after performing ancestral rites at this place. The place became famous as Gaya or Gayasirsha where all the Deities including the Trinity Lords reside always.

Legend related to Dharmashila :-

There was a sage by name Marichi who was the son of Lord Brahma who got married to a person by name Dharmavratha. One day she was washing her husband Marichi’s feet after he returned from forest. At that time Lord Brahma appeared there suddenly. Dharmavratha was in a fix as to whom to attend first. Finally she decided to attend to Lord Brahma first. This action angered sage Marichi and he cursed her of becoming a stone. Dharmavratha got very much disturbed with her husband’s action and started praying Lord Maha Vishnu who appeared in front of her. Dharmavratha requested Lord Vishnu to reverse the curse given by her husband.

Since Marichi was a very powerful sage, Lord Vishnu told her that the curse could not be reversed. Instead it would be converted into a boon by making the stone very sacred and celestial to all the Gods and also ensure that all the Gods reside in it. This was the same stone that was kept on the body of Gayasura when he was killed, on which Lord Vishnu had stepped with his foot. By the presence of all Deities in it the stone became very sacred and celestial to be known as Dharmashila. It is said that even a touch of this Dharmashila at Gaya Kshetra in Vishnupada Temple would result in salvation.

Legend related to Gaya Mahatmya
(Significance of ancestral rites at Gaya)

In olden times there lived a sage by name Dhaibhya who once went to Gaya Kshetra and performed sacred rites (Pinda Pradhana) to his forefathers with utmost devotion and after that started doing penance at this place. One day while he was doing penance a cosmic plane appeared before him and a divine person got down from it and asked him why was he doing this penance? Then the sage Dhaibhya in reply asked the cosmic person to disclose his details.

The cosmic person told the sage that he was the Brahma Manasa Puthra and brother of Rudra called Sanathkumara who lives in one of the urdhva lokas (Jano loka). He further said, O’ Sage “you have performed Pinda Pradhana at Gaya Kshetra with the result the entire Brahma Vamsa got the benefit and I have come here to bless you and show my affinity towards you.” On further questioning by sage as to how his action had benefited, Sanathkumara started narrating an incident related to Gaya Mahatmya.

In olden times there lived a king called Vishala who was a highly spiritual and religious minded person ruling his kingdom in Dharma Marga. His only shortfall was lack of children. On being advised by his purohits the king went to Gaya Kshetra and performed sacred rites to his forefathers (Pinda Dana, Thila Tharpana). While doing so there appeared three persons in the sky who were in three different colours (white, red and black) and they started glaring at the King with love and affection.

On being asked the white coloured person started telling that, “he was his father, the red coloured person was his grand father who had committed lot of sins while he was alive and the black coloured person was his great grand father who also had committed similar worst sins during his life time. Due to this they were suffering in the hell. Because of good deeds done, I have (white coloured person) acquired the heavenly status.” Now, due to your visit to the Gaya Kshetra and performing sacred rites (Pinda daana) your grand father and great grand father have been released from the hell and have joined me in the heaven. Thus you are responsible for the liberation of your forefathers from the hell by performing Pinda Pradhana and Tharpana at Gaya Kshetra. Now we are happily going to Pitru Loka and have come here to see you and bless you.

After this incident the king Vishala returned to his kingdom and soon was blessed with a son. Hence, this place (Gaya) has acquired lot of significance and Lord Maha Vishnu holding mace in his hand is residing here. Thus spoke Sanathkumara to the sage Dhaibhya and disappeared.

Legend of Sita Devi's Curse to Phalgu River

The story goes like this. During the Ramayana Lord Sri Rama along with his consort Goddess Sita Devi and his brother Lakshmana visited Gaya Kshetra for performing sacred rites to his forefathers (Dasaratha and others). While the brothers were taking bath Sita Devi was sitting on the banks of the river and playing with sand. Suddenly Dasaratha (father of Sri Rama) appeared out of the sand and asked Sita Devi to offer Pindam. While Sita Devi asked him to wait till his sons come back and offer Pindam in traditional way, Dasaratha was not prepared to wait. Instead he asked Sita Devi to offer him the Pindam made up of sand that was in her hand. With no other option available Sita offered Dasaratha the Pindam made up of Sand with five witnesses to her action. The witnesses were Phalgu River, Akshaya Vatam, a Brahmin, a Cow and a Tulasi Plant.

In those days ancestors were arriving personally to collect their share of sacred rites. When Sri Rama returned and started the rituals his father Dasaratha did not appear and he wondered as to why. Sita then told him as to what has happened and when Sri Rama did not believe she asked the witnesses to tell the truth. None but the Akshaya Vat told the truth to Sri Rama.In her anger Sita cursed the other four to the effect that the river Phalgu henceforth would not have water at Gaya, the Cow would no longer be worshipped from the front, there would be no Tulasi Plants in Gaya and Gaya Brahmins would never get satisfied and would always crave for more and more. Since Akshayavata revealed the truth Sita Devi blessed her that thenceforth who ever comes to Gaya for performing sacred rites would also perform the Pinda Pradanam at the site of Akshaya Vata.

Other stories related to Gaya :-

It is said that when the demon Gayasura was killed by Lord Maha Vishnu the body was cut into three parts out of which the upper portion had fallen at Gaya (Bihar) called Siro Gaya or Seersha Gaya, the middle portion had fallen at Jajpur (Orissa) called Nabhi Gaya and the bottom portion had fallen at Pithapuram (Andhra Pradesh) called Paada Gaya. As per another script the three places are Siro Gaya (Kapali Gaya) at Badrinath, Nabhi Gaya at Naimisharanya and the Paada Gaya at Gaya (near Patna in Bihar).

It is said that as per mythology, there are five Gaya Kshetras. They are Pithru Gaya (Siro Gaya) at Gaya (Bihar) on the banks of river Phalgu, Mathru Gaya at Siddhpur (Gujarat), Nabhi Gaya at Jajpur (Orissa) on the banks of Vaitharani river, Paada Gaya at Pithapuram (Andhra Pradesh) and Kapali Gaya at Badrinath. It is believed and said that Lord Parashurama (Dynamic Avathara of Lord Vishnu) had performed Pinda daan to his mother at Siddhpur.

Conclusion :-

Gaya is one of the great places of pilgrimage in India and has attained special sanctity among the Hindus and Hindu religion who strongly believe that it is incumbent on every Hindu to visit Gaya and make offerings to the departed souls of his ancestors. Mythologically described as the last among the three pillars in the “Holy Bridge to the Heaven” and praised as the most sacred place for ancestral rituals, the city Gaya has existed since time immemorial with its traditions of ancestral rites.

Creamy Mushroom Truffle Pasta

20 mins • 4 servings • Vegetarian

Luxurious restaurant-quality pasta made in under 20 minutes with real truffle oil.

Ingredients

  • 300g tagliatelle or fettuccine
  • 200g mixed mushrooms (shiitake, cremini)
  • 3 garlic cloves, minced
  • 200ml heavy cream
  • 50g Parmesan, grated
  • 1 tbsp truffle oil
  • Fresh parsley & black pepper

Instructions

  1. Cook pasta in salted water until al dente.
  2. Sauté mushrooms in butter until golden (5 mins).
  3. Add garlic, then pour in cream. Simmer 3 mins.
  4. Toss in cooked pasta + Parmesan.
  5. Drizzle with truffle oil, top with parsley.

Rainbow Buddha Bowl

15 mins • 2 servings • Vegan

Colorful, nourishing bowl packed with plant-based goodness and creamy tahini dressing.

Ingredients

  • 1 cup cooked quinoa
  • 1 sweet potato, roasted
  • 1 avocado, sliced
  • Handful cherry tomatoes
  • Shredded red cabbage
  • Chickpeas, roasted
  • Tahini + lemon dressing

Instructions

  1. Roast sweet potato cubes at 200°C for 20 mins.
  2. Cook quinoa according to package.
  3. Arrange all ingredients in a bowl by color.
  4. Drizzle generously with tahini-lemon dressing.
  5. Sprinkle with sesame seeds and enjoy!

Healthy Chocolate Avocado Mousse

10 mins • 4 servings • Vegan • No Sugar

Rich, creamy chocolate dessert made with avocado — tastes like pure indulgence!

Ingredients

  • 2 ripe avocados
  • 1/4 cup cocoa powder
  • 1/4 cup maple syrup or honey
  • 1/4 cup almond milk
  • 1 tsp vanilla extract
  • Pinch of sea salt

Instructions

  1. Blend all ingredients until silky smooth.
  2. Taste and adjust sweetness.
  3. Chill for 30 minutes (optional).
  4. Serve with berries and shaved chocolate.
